title: ACCY 6900 — Handout #2 Timeline
subtitle: Learn the U.S. accounting timeline
source: Teaching quiz for Handout #2 only (1787–2010). Each card explains the event first, then checks that you understood it. Same two-in-a-row rules as the other quizzes.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: Why does the Handout #2 timeline begin with the Constitution of 1787 instead of with Pacioli or the first CPA exam?

choices.text: Because 1787 is when double-entry bookkeeping was invented in Philadelphia
Because a functioning federal government is the platform later tax, banking, securities, and licensing rules would stand on
Because the SEC was created in 1787
Because New York licensed the first CPAs that year

questions.explanation:
The timeline is a story of public power responding to private abuse. None of that works without a government that can actually govern.

The Articles of Confederation failed that test. The 1787 Constitution created a federal system strong enough, over time, to tax (Civil War; later the income tax), regulate railroads and monopolies, license professions through the states, and eventually create the Fed, FTC, and SEC.

Slavery is flagged as an immense problem the founding did not solve. The handout still treats the federal design as effective enough to be the starting point for U.S. accounting history.
questions.lesson:
Handout #2 is a U.S. timeline of how accounting, auditing, and financial regulation grew up. It does not start with bookkeeping. It starts with government, because later tax laws, banking rules, securities laws, and CPA licensing all assume there is a working federal system that can write and enforce rules.

After independence, the country first tried the Articles of Confederation. That national government was too weak: it could not tax or coordinate well, and the states behaved almost like separate countries. In 1787 a new Constitution was written. The handout notes immense problems, especially slavery, but says the federal system proved effective.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: What problem with the Articles of Confederation does the handout say made a new constitution necessary?

choices.text: The Articles gave the president too much power over Wall Street
Government was unable to function adequately
The Articles banned all taxes, which made the Civil War impossible
The Articles created the SEC too early

questions.explanation:
If you remember only one phrase from this row of the timeline, remember “unable to function adequately.”

That is the handout’s reason for 1787. Later rows keep repeating the same pattern at a smaller scale: when a system cannot function (weak audits, weak banking rules, weak disclosure), lawmakers rewrite the rules.
questions.lesson: The Articles of Confederation were the United States’ first national charter. Under them, the central government lacked the tools it needed to function: it could not reliably raise money or make the states act together. The 1787 Constitution was written because that arrangement had already failed.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: What was Tammany Hall in the handout’s timeline?

choices.text: The first national board that wrote GAAP
New York City’s Democratic political machine, a long-running source of power and corruption that other governments copied
The federal agency that licensed CPAs in 1896
A Wall Street stock exchange created after the Civil War

questions.explanation:
Tammany Hall is in an accounting timeline because corruption is a demand driver for accounting.

When public money, contracts, and votes can be bought, someone eventually asks for books, audits, and rules that make the stealing visible. The handout is planting that idea early: American government and American business grew up with organized corruption, not after it.
questions.lesson: A political machine is an organized party operation that holds power by dispensing jobs, contracts, and favors, often with corruption attached. The handout’s example is Tammany Hall, New York City’s Democratic machine from the early 19th century. It became a long-term source of power and corruption, and other local and state governments copied the model nationwide.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: According to the timeline, Union financing of the Civil War required which pair of changes?

choices.text: Creation of the SEC and the PCAOB
Substantial new tax laws and an updated banking system regulated by the Treasury
A ban on auditor advertising and a federal CPA license
Adoption of IFRS and a junk-bond market

questions.explanation:
This is the first time the timeline ties money, tax, and banking together.

Taxes create a reason to measure income. A Treasury-regulated banking system creates a reason to measure capital, reserves, and notes. Accounting is useful in peacetime; it becomes unavoidable when a government must raise and track huge sums.

The CPA profession does not appear until 1896, but the federal need for reliable numbers starts here.
questions.lesson: Wars are expensive. The Union side of the Civil War (1861–1865) could not pay for armies with the old, tiny federal toolkit. The handout says Union financing required two big institutional changes: substantial new tax laws, and an updated banking system regulated by the Treasury Department.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: Which two federal moves does the handout group as the start of U.S. market regulation in this era?

choices.text: The Securities Acts of 1933 and 1934
The Interstate Commerce Commission Act of 1887 and the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890
Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank
The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and Regulation FD

questions.explanation:
Before there is an SEC, there is railroad and monopoly regulation.

The ICC (1887) is about a network industry that could overcharge shippers. Sherman (1890) is about concentrated private power. Both require financial facts: what does the railroad earn, what does Standard Oil control, how is the trust financed?

Accounting is already becoming a public tool, not just a merchant’s private notebook.
questions.lesson: By the late 1800s, railroads and industrial trusts (huge combinations of companies) dominated the economy. In 1887 Congress created the Interstate Commerce Commission to regulate railroads. In 1890 the Sherman Antitrust Act let the federal government attack monopolies. The handout’s “wins” include breaking up the Northern Pacific Railroad and Rockefeller’s Standard Oil.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: How did the first U.S. CPA licenses, in New York from 1896, get issued?

choices.text: By presidential appointment after a Senate hearing
Based on experience and written exam results
Automatically to anyone who worked at a railroad
By the SEC after a 10-K review

questions.explanation:
1896 is the profession’s birthday in this timeline.

Licensing says: not everyone who can add is an auditor. You need supervised experience and you need to pass an exam. That is how a craft becomes a profession.

Notice what has not happened yet. There is still no SEC, no FASB, no PCAOB. The states, not Washington, created the CPA.
questions.lesson: A certified public accountant (CPA) is a state-licensed professional allowed to audit other people’s books and, eventually, to sign opinions that outsiders rely on. The handout says New York was the first U.S. state to grant that license, starting in 1896. The test was not a political appointment. It was experience plus a written exam. Every other state later copied the idea.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the handout’s 19th-century order?

choices.text: CPA licensing, then the Constitution, then Sherman
Constitution, political machines, Civil War finance, railroad/antitrust laws, then CPA licensing
Sherman Act, then Tammany Hall, then the Articles of Confederation
SEC, then CPA licensing, then the Civil War

questions.explanation:
Order matters because each step creates the next demand.

A federal government can tax and charter banks. Taxes and banks need books. Railroads and trusts need regulation, which needs books. Once outsiders rely on those books, states invent a licensed auditor.

If you reverse the order (CPAs before a federal government, or the SEC in the 1800s), you are mixing later chapters into this one.
questions.lesson:
Put the 19th-century rows in order in your head: 1787 Constitution → political machines and corruption → Civil War tax and Treasury banking → 1887/1890 railroad and antitrust regulation → 1896 CPA licensing.

The pattern is: public power expands as private and political abuse becomes visible, and a licensed measuring profession appears once there is something important to measure.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: What does the handout say the 1913–1914 burst of federal reform followed?

choices.text: The Enron hearings
The Pujo hearings
The Teapot Dome criminal trial
The McKesson & Robbins inventory counts

questions.explanation:
Think of 1913–1914 as the Progressive Era’s financial package.

Income tax (16th Amendment) gives Washington a permanent claim on private profits, which is why tax accounting becomes a career. The Federal Reserve is a central bank: it can create liquidity and supervise banks. The FTC polices unfair competition. Clayton tightens antitrust.

The trigger in this handout is not a single corporate fraud. It is a congressional investigation of concentrated finance.
questions.lesson: The Pujo hearings (named for Congressman Arsène Pujo) were 1912–1913 investigations into the “money trust”: a small circle of New York bankers who seemed to control credit. The handout says substantial federal reform followed in 1913–1914: a permanent federal income tax (Sixteenth Amendment), the Federal Reserve, the Federal Trade Commission, and new antitrust law including the Clayton Act.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: In the 1913–1914 cluster, which reform most directly created a lasting federal demand for income measurement?

choices.text: The Clayton Act’s ban on interlocking directorates only
The Sixteenth Amendment’s permanent federal income tax
The lifting of the auditor advertising ban
The creation of the PCAOB

questions.explanation:
Antitrust and the Fed matter for markets. The income tax matters for the definition of income itself.

Once Washington taxes profits, accounting choices (when is revenue earned? what is deductible?) become legal questions, not just management questions. That is a second profession-building force beside CPA licensing.
questions.lesson: The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) let Congress tax income. Before that, federal money came mostly from tariffs and excises. A permanent income tax means the government cares how “income” is measured, year after year, for millions of people and firms.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: Which pair was created in the 1913–1914 reforms listed in the timeline?

choices.text: The SEC and the PCAOB
The Federal Reserve System and the Federal Trade Commission
The FASB and the IASB
The Resolution Trust Corporation and TARP

questions.explanation:
Do not jump ahead to 1934 (SEC) or 2002 (PCAOB). In 1913–1914 Washington built a central bank and a competition watchdog.

The Fed will return in this timeline as the crisis firefighter (LTCM, Bear Stearns, Lehman aftermath, AIG, TARP-era liquidity). The FTC is the cousin of antitrust, not of securities disclosure.
questions.lesson: The Federal Reserve System (1913) is the U.S. central bank. It was created so the country would not depend on a handful of private New York bankers for credit in a panic. The Federal Trade Commission (1914) is a civilian agency that polices unfair methods of competition. Both appear in the same 1913–1914 row as the income tax and Clayton Act.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: What made Ponzi’s 1920 operation a “Ponzi scheme” as the handout describes it?

choices.text: He hid inventory in oil tankers filled with water
He promised huge, fast returns and paid early people with money from later people in order to recruit still more
He capitalized WorldCom’s line costs as assets
He backdated stock options at dozens of companies

questions.explanation:
Learn the mechanics, not just the name.

Step 1: promise an impossible or implausible return. Step 2: pay the first arrivals so they become advertisements. Step 3: take the next arrivals’ cash to fund those payouts. Step 4: collapse when recruitment fails.

Ponzi used postal reply coupons as the cover story and was gone in months. Eighty-eight years later, Bernard Madoff will run the same logic for decades. Same species, different scale.
questions.lesson:
A Ponzi scheme pays old investors with money taken from new investors. There is no real engine of profit, or not enough of one. The scheme dies when new cash slows down.

Charles Ponzi (1920) promised a 50% return in 45 days using International Reply Coupons (postal vouchers that could, in theory, be bought cheap in one country and redeemed dear in another). He paid early “investors” so they would brag and recruit. He was shut down within months after collecting millions, imprisoned, and deported to Italy.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: What return did Ponzi promise, and how quickly?

choices.text: 2% a year, like a savings account
A 50% return in 45 days
150 years of compound interest
A 16th Amendment tax refund in 1913

questions.explanation:
The numbers are memorable on purpose.

50% in 45 days is not “a good year in the market.” It is a billboard that the economics cannot be real. Paying early investors is how the billboard stays lit. Prison and deportation are how the 1920 chapter ends. The idea of the scheme does not end; it waits for Madoff.
questions.lesson: Ponzi’s cover story was International Reply Coupons, not a hedge fund or a gas-trading operation. He promised 50% in 45 days. That speed is part of the tell: legitimate businesses rarely advertise guaranteed 50% returns in a month and a half.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: Who took the bribes at the center of Teapot Dome, and what happened when the scheme was found out?

choices.text: Charles Ponzi; he was deported immediately
Interior Secretary Albert Fall; the oil leases were cancelled and he was jailed for bribery
Bernie Ebbers; WorldCom restated $11 billion
Tino De Angelis; salad-oil tankers were seized by the Fed

questions.explanation:
Teapot Dome is about public office for sale.

The product being stolen is not a fake receivable. It is access to national oil reserves through a Cabinet secretary. Cancellation of the leases plus jail for Fall is the handout’s resolution.

Compare it with Tammany Hall: both are political corruption. Teapot Dome is federal, spectacular, and ends in a criminal conviction of a Cabinet officer.
questions.lesson: Teapot Dome is a government corruption scandal, not a corporate earnings fraud. The handout says Warren G. Harding’s presidency was essentially “bought” by oil interests. The Interior Department leased the Teapot Dome oil reserve (and other oil properties) to oilmen in exchange for bribes to Interior Secretary Albert Fall. When it was discovered, the leases were cancelled and Fall went to jail for bribery.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: In the Ultramares case, what had the auditor done that set up the lawsuit?

choices.text: Refused to issue any opinion
Given an unqualified opinion even though substantial fraud was present
Created the SEC without congressional approval
Observed inventory and confirmed receivables, which later became banned

questions.explanation:
This is the timeline’s first famous auditor-liability case.

A lender used audited numbers to decide whether to extend credit. The numbers were rotten. The auditor had still signed a clean opinion. The legal question is not “was there fraud at the company?” It is “does the auditor owe that lender a recovery?”
questions.lesson: An audit opinion is the auditor’s public conclusion on the financial statements. An unqualified (clean) opinion says, in substance, the statements are fairly presented. In Ultramares (1924), auditor Touche Niven gave that clean opinion even though substantial fraud was present. Ultramares, a lender who had relied on the statements, sued the auditor.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: What did the Ultramares court conclude about Touche?

choices.text: Touche was fraudulent, so it had to pay the lender in full
Touche was negligent but not fraudulent, and therefore not liable
Touche had violated Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404
Touche was innocent because CPAs did not exist yet

questions.explanation:
Carry this sentence with you: negligent but not fraudulent, therefore not liable.

To a student, that sounds like a loophole. To the 1924 legal world, it was a line: ordinary third parties could not treat a careless audit as if the auditor had guaranteed the loan.

Later, Continental Vending (1969) will show the opposite edge: even following GAAS may not save you from criminal fraud charges if the statements are known to be false. Ultramares is about civil liability to a lender. Continental Vending is about criminal guilt.
questions.lesson: Courts distinguish negligence (carelessness; you should have done better) from fraud (you intended to deceive, or you were so reckless that the law treats it as deceit). In Ultramares, the court found Touche negligent but not fraudulent, and therefore not liable to the lender. That distinction became a landmark limit on who can sue auditors, and for what.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: What did the Securities Acts of 1933–1934 create, and for what two purposes does the handout name?

choices.text: The FASB, to replace the APB
The SEC, to regulate securities markets and provide adequate disclosures of public corporations’ finances
The PCAOB, to inspect audits of private companies only
The Federal Reserve, to set income-tax rates

questions.explanation:
1933–1934 is the disclosure revolution.

Before the SEC, a public company’s finances could be a private conversation among insiders. After the SEC, periodic public reporting is a legal duty. That is why 10-Ks, 10-Qs, and audited financials become central to the profession.

The SEC does not yet write all of GAAP itself in this story; it will later look to private-sector boards (CAP, APB, FASB). But it is the cop on the securities beat.
questions.lesson:
The 1929 crash and the investigations that followed convinced Congress that Wall Street and many corporations had been a swamp of abuse. Under Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 created the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

The SEC’s job in this handout is twofold: regulate securities markets, and require adequate disclosure of public corporations’ finances. Disclosure means outsiders can see the numbers, not that the numbers are guaranteed true.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: Why, according to the handout, was the McKesson & Robbins fraud able to continue for years?

choices.text: The SEC had already approved the fake inventory
Auditor Price Waterhouse did not audit inventory or receivables
The company used special purpose entities the way Enron later would
Charles Ponzi was the CFO

questions.explanation:
If you do not look at the stuff, and you do not ask the customers, a liar can invent both the warehouse and the customers.

Inventory observation and receivable confirmation sound boring. McKesson is why they became mandatory. The failure is not “PW missed a subtle judgment.” It is “PW skipped the two accounts that were entirely fake.”
questions.lesson: McKesson & Robbins (1937) was a pharmaceutical company whose president ran a massive fraud: inventory that did not exist, and receivables (money customers supposedly owed) that did not exist. Price Waterhouse was the auditor. The fraud ran for years because PW did not audit inventory or receivables. The public demand that followed was for audit regulation, not just better manners.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: What did the 1939 Committee on Audit Procedures require first?

choices.text: A ban on all auditor advertising
Physical inventory observation and confirmation of receivables
Creation of the FASB’s seven board seats
Internet simulcasts of earnings calls

questions.explanation:
This is cause and effect in one pair of dates: 1937 fraud, 1939 procedure.

“Physically conduct inventory” means go to the warehouse. “Confirm receivables” means ask the customer, in writing, whether the balance is real. You are no longer allowed to take management’s word for the two accounts McKesson invented.

Auditing standards here are a private-sector committee’s answer. Seventy years later, SOX will put a public board (the PCAOB) over public-company audit standards.
questions.lesson: After McKesson, the Committee on Audit Procedures was established in 1939 to issue auditing standards. Its first move, in this handout, was to require auditors to physically conduct (observe) inventory and to confirm receivables with the supposed customers. Those procedures are still core fieldwork.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: How did the Committee on Accounting Procedures set GAAP from 1938 to 1959?

choices.text: By Staff Accounting Bulletins issued as criminal indictments
By Accounting Research Bulletins; 51 ARBs over about 20 years
By IFRS, which the United States adopted in 1938
By Yellow Book chapters from the GAO

questions.explanation:
CAP is the first named U.S. GAAP factory in this timeline.

It is a committee of the profession, not a government agency. ARBs are the product. 51 documents in 20 years is a lot of rule-writing, and the handout’s point is that the foundations of today’s GAAP start here.

CAP will be replaced because the process, not only the rules, came to look inadequate.
questions.lesson: GAAP means generally accepted accounting principles: the rules for how companies measure and present results. In 1938 the Committee on Accounting Procedures (CAP) was created to establish GAAP. Its vehicle was the Accounting Research Bulletin (ARB). The handout says 51 ARBs were issued over 20 years (1938–1959). Many became fundamental standards still in the DNA of U.S. GAAP, even though the particulars changed.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: What is the handout’s verdict on the Accounting Principles Board that replaced CAP in 1959?

choices.text: It immediately solved every standard-setting problem and still sets GAAP today
It used new procedures but kept many of the problems of CAP
It was a criminal court for auditors
It created the Federal Reserve

questions.explanation:
Standard-setting has a succession: CAP (1938) → APB (1959) → FASB (1973).

Each replacement is an admission that the last process lost legitimacy. APB is the awkward middle child: new procedures, old problems. FASB will be sold as better process, governance, and public involvement.

If an exam asks “who writes GAAP now?”, the timeline’s answer after 1973 is FASB, not CAP or APB.
questions.lesson: In 1959 the Accounting Principles Board (APB) replaced CAP. The handout also misspells it “ABP” in one place; it means APB. New procedures were used, but “many of the problems of the previous organization” remained. So 1959 is not a happy ending. It is a halfway reform.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: Which pairing is correct in this era?

choices.text: 1934 PCAOB writes audit standards; 1938 SEC writes tax law
1933–34 SEC for disclosure; 1938 CAP for GAAP; 1939 audit procedures after McKesson; 1959 APB replaces CAP
1959 Ultramares creates the income tax
1937 FASB replaces the Fed

questions.explanation:
Students mix these bodies because they all sound like alphabet soup. Separate them by job.

SEC: public markets and disclosure. CAP/APB/FASB: measurement rules (GAAP). Committee on Audit Procedures (later other audit bodies, then PCAOB for public companies): how to audit. McKesson is the horror story that connects disclosure to fieldwork.
questions.lesson: Hold the 1930s–1950s machinery in one picture. Congress creates the SEC (1933–34) to force disclosure. A corporate fraud (McKesson, 1937) shows that disclosure is worthless if the auditor never looks. 1938 CAP starts writing GAAP. 1939 audit procedures start requiring looking. 1959 APB tries to replace CAP and only partly succeeds.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: How did Allied Crude fool the people who thought they were confirming salad-oil collateral?

choices.text: By using Enron-style special purpose entities
By filling tankers with water and topping them off with salad oil, so inspectors confirmed “oil”
By capitalizing WorldCom’s operating expenses
By backdating stock options to a low price date

questions.explanation:
McKesson taught “go look at the inventory.” Salad oil teaches “looking is not enough if you look stupidly.”

A dipstick in a tank of water with an oil film still “proves” oil if you never ask what is underneath. Confirmation of form (there is a tank; there is a paperwork shipment) is not confirmation of substance (there is salad oil).

De Angelis’s seven years in jail is the personal ending. The professional lesson is skepticism about what an inspection has actually observed.
questions.lesson: The Great Salad Oil Swindle (1963) is almost a cartoon, which is why it teaches. Allied Crude Vegetable Oil filled tankers with water and poured a layer of salad oil on top. Inspectors for creditors “confirmed shipments of salad oil.” Creditors lost millions. CEO Tino De Angelis spent seven years in jail.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: What is the unsettling holding of Continental Vending in this timeline?

choices.text: Auditors can never be sued by lenders
Three auditors were guilty of criminal fraud even though the firm did not violate GAAS
Salad-oil inspectors were promoted to the Supreme Court
The SEC was abolished

questions.explanation:
GAAS is a professional checklist. Criminal fraud is about deceit.

Continental Vending says you can follow the standards and still go to prison if you certify statements you know are false. “We did the procedures” is not a magic shield.

Set it next to Ultramares (1924): that case limited civil liability where the auditor was merely negligent. This case imposes criminal guilt where the statements were known to be false. Different axes: who can collect money vs. who can lose liberty.
questions.lesson: Continental Vending (1969) is a criminal case against auditors, not a civil lender lawsuit like Ultramares. Lybrand, Ross Bros. & Montgomery (a Big Eight ancestor of today’s firms) certified financial statements known to be false. The shocking line in the handout: Lybrand did not violate GAAS (generally accepted auditing standards), yet three Lybrand auditors were found guilty of criminal fraud.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: Why was FASB created in 1973?

choices.text: To prosecute Albert Fall
To replace the APB with improved process, governance, and public involvement
To bail out savings and loans
To inspect every public-company audit the way the PCAOB later would

questions.explanation:
FASB is the third GAAP factory: CAP → APB → FASB.

“Process, governance, and public involvement” means: not a closed club of the same firms writing rules for themselves without due process. Independent board, public comments, a conceptual framework later on.

FASB does not inspect audits. That public-company job will belong to the PCAOB after 2002. Do not merge those institutions.
questions.lesson: In 1973 the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) was established to replace the APB. The selling points in the handout are not “smarter accountants.” They are improved process, governance, and public involvement. FASB is still the private-sector GAAP writer the SEC looks to in the U.S.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: Besides banning bribery of foreign officials for business, what else did the FCPA mandate?

choices.text: That all U.S. firms adopt IFRS immediately
Internal control requirements for public firms
The end of CPA licensing
A $180 billion equity injection into AIG

questions.explanation:
FCPA is not only an anti-bribery criminal statute. It is an early internal-control statute for public companies.

That second half is the bridge to Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 a generation later: management (and, after SOX, auditors) must take the control system seriously, not only the face of the income statement.

1977: controls become federal law. 2002: controls become a certified, inspectable duty.
questions.lesson: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) of 1977 has two halves, and students often remember only the first. After bribery scandals involving foreign officials, Congress made it illegal to bribe foreign officials for business purposes. The same Act also mandated internal control requirements for public firms. Internal control means the company’s own systems to authorize, record, and safeguard transactions.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: What does the handout mean by “lowballing” after the 1979 advertising-ban lift?

choices.text: Overcharging so that only rich clients can be audited
A very low bid to get a new client, which helped turn audits into a priced commodity
Refusing to bid on SEC registrants
Paying Ponzi returns to partners

questions.explanation:
A commodity is something buyers pick by price because they think the product is the same everywhere. If audits are sold that way, the winning firm may cut hours, staff, or skepticism to make the cheap fee work.

The handout is careful: “possibly” lower quality. It is not a lab proof. It is a warning that independence and effort are hard to sustain when the engagement was won by being cheapest.

Remember the date: 1979 is culture and competition, not a new accounting standard.
questions.lesson: Until 1979, audit firms in the U.S. were not supposed to advertise. Federal pressure forced the profession to lift that ban. The unintended consequence, says the handout, was “lowballing”: bidding a very low fee to win the client. Through the 1980s and beyond, the audit was priced more and more as a commodity, possibly resulting in lower-quality audits.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: Which statement best captures this stretch of the timeline?

choices.text: Nothing important happens between Ultramares and Enron
Frauds expose weak inspection and weak ethics, while the institutions of GAAP, internal control, and audit pricing are all rewritten
The SEC is created in 1973 to replace FASB
CPA licensing begins in 1977 in California only

questions.explanation:
This is the professionalization decade-plus.

The measurement board gets rebuilt (FASB). The law starts caring about control systems (FCPA). The business model of the audit firm changes (advertising and lowballing). Meanwhile two scandals say: looking isn’t enough, and checking the GAAS box isn’t enough.
questions.lesson: Line up the 1960s–1970s lessons. Salad oil (1963): observation can be fooled. Continental Vending (1969): GAAS is not a criminal defense. FASB (1973): new GAAP governance. FCPA (1977): bribery plus internal control. Advertising (1979): price competition and lowballing.

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: What does the handout say Garn-St. Germain (1982) did, and what was the longer-run result?

choices.text: It created the SEC; markets became safer forever
It deregulated S&Ls to avoid immediate bankruptcies, but helped produce a corrupt industry, mass failure, jailings, and a federal bailout
It banned junk bonds and saved Drexel Burnham
It required physical inventory observation

questions.explanation:
Deregulation here is a painkiller, not a cure.

Rising rates made the old S&L model insolvent. Congress loosened the rules so institutions could chase new, riskier profits. Some of those bets were fraud. The bill for that arrives at the end of the decade as the RTC bailout.

Whenever a timeline says “we deregulated to avoid bankruptcy,” ask what behavior the new freedom rewarded.
questions.lesson: Savings and loans (S&Ls) were depositor-funded lenders, many of them focused on home mortgages. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, interest rates soared. S&Ls were stuck earning old, low mortgage rates while they had to pay high rates to keep deposits. The Garn-St. Germain Act (1982) deregulated them to stave off immediate bankruptcy. The handout’s judgment: that helped in the short run but created a soon-to-be corrupt industry that would need a federal bailout. Much of the industry failed; dozens of executives were jailed.

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: Besides making a market in junk bonds, what does the handout charge Milken with?

choices.text: Inventing double-entry bookkeeping
A vast criminal conspiracy including price-data manipulation, insider trading, illegal deals, and tax fraud, which also sank Drexel Burnham
Running Fannie Mae into conservatorship by himself
Writing the Sarbanes-Oxley Act

questions.explanation:
A market-maker is supposed to stand ready to buy and sell so that others can trade. That can be legitimate. The handout’s Milken is a market-maker plus a criminal enterprise.

Drexel Burnham is the firm that goes down with him. Keep this separate from the S&L story: both are 1980s finance, but Milken is junk-bond Wall Street, not a Midwestern thrift.
questions.lesson: Junk bonds are high-yield, high-risk bonds: the issuer is less creditworthy, so investors demand more interest. Michael Milken, in the 1980s, specialized in making a market in them. The handout does not treat him as a mere innovator. It says he multiplied wealth by manipulating price data, insider trading, illegal outside deals, tax fraud, and other pieces of a vast criminal conspiracy. His downfall also forced Drexel Burnham into bankruptcy.

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: Who was ZZZZ Best’s founder, and how does the handout date his fall?

choices.text: Al Dunlap, jailed in 1998 with Sunbeam
Barry Minkow, jailed in 1989 after building the company on increasing fraud
Ken Lay, acquitted in 2001
Albert Fall, deported to Italy in 1920

questions.explanation:
Minkow is the 1980s version of “the growth story was the fraud.”

Insurance restoration is a real business. Fake restoration contracts are a receivable-and-revenue fiction, cousin to McKesson’s fake customers. Jail in 1989 closes the row. Do not confuse Minkow with Dunlap (Sunbeam), Ebbers (WorldCom), or Kozlowski (Tyco).
questions.lesson: ZZZZ Best (1986) was a small insurance-restoration company: it claimed to rebuild properties after fires and other damage. Founder Barry Minkow made it look successful with increasing levels of fraud. He was jailed in 1989. The lesson is not size. A small company with a charismatic founder can still manufacture revenue.

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: What cleanup vehicle closed the failed S&Ls, and what does the handout say taxpayers lost?

choices.text: The PCAOB; about $11 billion
The RTC (Resolution Trust Corporation); almost $100 billion
The FASB; $1.6 billion, like the later AIG fine
TARP in 1934; $180 billion

questions.explanation:
Connect 1982 to 1989. Garn-St. Germain postponed death; it did not prevent a corrupt boom. Then the government becomes the world’s worst asset manager: take over 700-plus dead thrifts, sell the pieces, eat a ~$100 billion loss.

The RTC is a temporary warehouse for failed-institution assets. TARP (2008) will be a different tool: capital for living banks. Do not swap the acronyms.
questions.lesson: The S&L crisis, with substantial fraud, failed more than 700 savings and loans. They were closed by the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC). The handout labels it the “Regulation Trust Corporation”; the actual name is Resolution Trust Corporation. The RTC sold billions of dollars of S&L assets. Taxpayers were left with a net loss of almost $100 billion. The cleanup runs 1989 into the early 1990s.

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: What did the 1995 litigation-reform statute do to auditors, in the handout’s telling?

choices.text: It created criminal liability for all clean opinions
It reduced their potential legal liabilities, which the handout links to more aggressive audits later in the 1990s
It banned CPA advertising again
It replaced FASB with the APB

questions.explanation:
Liability is a brake. If you can be ruined for a missed fraud, you may audit more cautiously (or refuse risky clients). If liability shrinks, the brake loosens.

The handout is drawing a straight line from a 1995 legal change to the 1997–2002 explosion of accounting scandals. You should treat that as the course’s causal story, whether or not every economist agrees.
questions.lesson: In 1995 Congress passed accountant-friendly litigation reform (the handout’s “Public Securities litigation Reform Act,” usually called the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, or PSLRA). It reduced potential legal liabilities of external auditors. The handout’s worry: that could produce more aggressive audits, “which seemed to be the result in the late 1990s and beyond.”

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: Which cause-and-effect chain is the one the timeline is telling?

choices.text: SOX in 1982 created the Fed, which then banned junk bonds
Deregulation and fraud blow up S&Ls; a huge public bailout follows; then auditor legal risk is reduced just before a wave of corporate accounting scandals
Pacioli in 1989 invented receivables confirmation
Ponzi in 1995 created TARP

questions.explanation:
This is the runway to Enron, not a random list.

Public losses at S&Ls show how costly bad accounting and bad incentives are. Then Congress, in 1995, eases auditor lawsuit risk. The next pages of the handout are Waste Management, Sunbeam, Cendant, Rite Aid, Enron, WorldCom. The handout wants you to feel that sequence as one story.
questions.lesson: The 1980s–mid-1990s block is: loosen S&Ls (1982) → junk-bond crime and Drexel (1980s) → Minkow (1986) → 700 S&Ls die and RTC costs ~$100 billion (1989–early 1990s) → 1995 law makes it harder to sue auditors.

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: Where did Waste Management’s fraud especially sit, and how large were the restatements in the handout?

choices.text: In Teapot Dome oil leases; $180 billion
In property, plant, and equipment; over $1 billion across five years, after which the firm failed
In International Reply Coupons; $50 in 45 days
In subprime CDO tranches; $30 billion of Fed guarantees

questions.explanation:
Revenue fraud is easy to picture (fake sales). PPE fraud is quieter: change an assumption about how long a truck lasts, and this year’s expense shrinks.

Overstated revenues plus understated expenses is the complete earnings recipe. A $1 billion-plus five-year restatement means the lie was not a one-quarter miss. Then failure: you cannot un-dump the trash on the income statement and keep the same stock-market story.
questions.lesson: Waste Management (1997) was a trash, landfill, and waste company. The handout calls that a metaphor for the accounting: overstated revenues, understated expenses, with a special focus on fraudulent accounting for property, plant, and equipment (PPE). PPE fraud often means stretching asset lives, inflating salvage values, or capitalizing costs that should be expenses, so depreciation stays too low and profits look too high. After restatements of over $1 billion covering five years, the firm failed.

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: What is the Sunbeam story in this timeline?

choices.text: A successful turnaround with no accounting issues
Al Dunlap’s turnaround profits were sustained by fraudulent revenue recognition; Sunbeam wrote off over $1 billion and went bankrupt
Barry Minkow’s insurance-restoration contracts were real
Dennis Kozlowski invented the Federal Reserve

questions.explanation:
A turnaround can be real (cut waste, sell more). Sunbeam’s reported turnaround was not.

Dunlap is the person to attach to this row, the way Minkow attaches to ZZZZ Best and Ebbers to WorldCom. The $1 billion write-off is the same order of magnitude as Waste Management’s restatement: late-1990s frauds are now measured in ten figures.
questions.lesson:
Sunbeam (1998) made appliances and was failing. It hired Al Dunlap, a famous cost-cutter, to turn it around. Costs were cut and profits rose, but the profits were maintained only by fraudulent revenue recognition and other illegal acts. The company had to write off over $1 billion from previous years before declaring bankruptcy.

Revenue recognition fraud means recording sales too early, too large, or that are not real sales (for example, stuffing channels or parking inventory).

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: What went wrong in the Cendant / CUC deal as the handout tells it?

choices.text: CUC was too small to matter
HFS bought CUC (and became Cendant) only to learn afterward that CUC’s books had been fraudulent for years
Cendant was the auditor of Ultramares
The Fed required HFS to acquire Lehman Brothers

questions.explanation:
Due diligence is supposed to include the accounting. Cendant is what happens when the target’s earnings were a multi-year fiction.

This is different from Waste Management (the company’s own PPE games) and Sunbeam (the company’s own revenue games). Here the fraud is imported through M&A. That is why later dealmakers obsess over quality of earnings.
questions.lesson: Cendant (1998) is an acquisition story. A conglomerate called HFS grew profits by buying other companies. It acquired CUC International and renamed the combination Cendant. Only after the deal closed did it become clear that CUC had used fraudulent accounting for years. The buyer inherited a lie.

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: Why did LTCM require a Fed-backed rescue in 1998?

choices.text: It had fake salad-oil inventory
Overextended leverage and disastrous hedges, including on the Russian ruble, threatened a wider financial blowup
It was the first post-SOX accounting scandal
It refused to follow Regulation FD

questions.explanation:
LTCM is not an earnings-restatement story. It is a leverage-and-contagion story.

Smart people plus huge borrowed money plus a wrong-way bet can still threaten everyone they traded with. The Fed’s interest is not saving the partners’ pride. It is stopping a chain reaction.

You will see this logic again in 2008 with Bear, Lehman, and AIG. 1998 is the dress rehearsal.
questions.lesson: Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM, 1998) was a giant hedge fund, reputed to be run by the smartest financial experts. It used enormous leverage (borrowed money piled on a small sliver of equity) and ended up on the wrong side of huge bets, including the Russian ruble (the handout says “rubble”) and other ill-advised hedges. A Federal Reserve–backed bailout was needed to unwind the positions and “protect the financial world.”

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: What followed Rite Aid’s accounting issues in the timeline?

choices.text: Creation of the original CAP board in 1938
Earnings restatements, SEC and other investigations and lawsuits, and executives fired and jailed
A successful IPO of International Reply Coupons
Immediate passage of the Sherman Act

questions.explanation:
By 1999 the late-1990s pipeline is fully open: restatement → SEC → civil suits → jail.

Rite Aid is useful because it shows the pattern is not reserved for energy traders and telecom giants. A drugstore chain can walk the same path.
questions.lesson: Rite Aid (1999), a drugstore chain, had several accounting issues. Those led to earnings restatements, SEC and other investigations, and lawsuits. Executives were fired and jailed. It is a smaller brand than Enron, but the pattern is the same: bad numbers, restatement, enforcement, personal punishment.

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: What problem was Regulation FD designed to stop?

choices.text: Physical observation of inventory
Companies giving material earnings news to favored analysts and insiders instead of to the public
The advertising of audit services
The creation of junk bonds

questions.explanation:
Disclosure can be unfair even when the numbers are honest.

If a star analyst gets the miss an hour early, that analyst’s clients trade on news the rest of the market does not have. FD is about equal access to the announcement, usually by putting the call on the internet.

It is not a GAAP standard and not an audit standard. It is a communications rule from the SEC, dated 2001, on the doorstep of Enron.
questions.lesson: Regulation FD (Fair Disclosure) in 2001 was an SEC rule against selective disclosure. Companies had been whispering earnings news to favored analysts and other investment insiders. FD required that when a company talks material information, the public hears it too. Earnings announcements were to be made public, usually through internet simulcasts.

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: Which theme ties this block together before Enron explodes?

choices.text: The profession had already solved fraud, so SOX was unnecessary
Earnings games, imported acquisition fraud, a leverage scare, and then a rule that markets must hear news at the same time
The only issue was Tammany Hall patronage in New York City
FASB was abolished and replaced by Ponzi

questions.explanation:
The handout is stacking kindling.

Corporate books are being cooked in several styles (PPE, revenue, M&A). A hedge fund shows that smart leverage can still need the Fed. FD tries to civilize the information game. Then Enron arrives as “possibly the biggest business scandal in American history.”
questions.lesson: Stack 1997–2001: Waste Management (PPE, $1B+, failure), Sunbeam (Dunlap, revenue recognition, $1B write-off, bankruptcy), Cendant (bought CUC’s hidden fraud), LTCM (leverage, Fed-backed unwind), Rite Aid (restatements, jail), Regulation FD (no more whispered earnings).

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: How does the handout say Enron kept the high-tech trading facade standing?

choices.text: By physically observing every pipeline each quarter
Through fraud including special purpose entities, derivatives, and deceptive trading profits
By following Continental Vending’s GAAS defense
By converting operating expenses into $11 billion of capital assets

questions.explanation:
Separate Enron from WorldCom. Enron is complexity: SPEs, derivatives, trading. WorldCom is simplicity: capitalize expenses that should have hit earnings.

An SPE can be a real bankruptcy-remote box. Enron’s were used to keep ugly items off the mothership’s balance sheet and to book income that was not economic. Derivatives can hedge; they can also mark a fantasy.

Jail for executives is the personal ending. Arthur Andersen’s destruction (not detailed in this handout row) is the professional earthquake. SOX is the statutory ending.
questions.lesson: Enron (2001) began as a stodgy gas-pipeline company and recast itself as a high-tech global trader. The facade, the handout says, was maintained through fraud: widespread special purpose entities (SPEs), derivatives, and deceptive use of trading profits. SPEs are legally separate vehicles; used honestly they isolate a project, used dishonestly they hide debt and manufacture earnings. The handout calls Enron possibly the biggest business scandal in American history. Several executives were jailed.

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: What was WorldCom’s core accounting fraud in the handout?

choices.text: Filling tankers with water and a skim of salad oil
Recording operating expenses as capital assets, some $11 billion; Bernie Ebbers was among those jailed
Paying 50% in 45 days with postal coupons
Backdating Fannie Mae’s stock options only

questions.explanation:
$11 billion is the number to remember, and “opex as capex” is the method.

If you spend $1 on a phone network’s ordinary costs and call it an asset, you have invented profit. Do that at industrial scale and you can postpone looking bankrupt.

Ebbers is the WorldCom name, as Kozlowski is Tyco and the Rigas family is Adelphia. These 2002 rows arrive together for a reason: they are the political fuel for Sarbanes-Oxley.
questions.lesson: WorldCom (2002) was a large telecom. When actual profits collapsed, it hid the collapse with a simple fraud: it recorded operating expenses as capital assets, about $11 billion worth. Capitalizing an expense moves a cost from the income statement (where it kills profit now) to the balance sheet (where it is depreciated slowly). CEO Bernie Ebbers was among the executives jailed.

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: What extra ingredient does Adelphia add on top of accounting fraud?

choices.text: It was the first CPA licensing statute
Governance abuse to benefit Rigas family members, with family/board insiders jailed and the company bankrupt
It successfully replaced the SEC
It was a pure hedge-fund leverage problem like LTCM with no family issues

questions.explanation:
Enron hid risk in SPEs. WorldCom hid costs in assets. Adelphia hid the fact that the public company was a family piggy bank.

When insiders sit on the board and the company pays their bills, independence is gone. Jail plus bankruptcy is the ending. SOX will answer with new rules on boards, audit committees, and related-party honesty.
questions.lesson: Adelphia (2002) was a cable-TV empire. Accounting fraud was used in part to cover corporate-governance violations that benefited Rigas family members (the handout spells it “Regas”). Adelphia went bankrupt. Several Rigas employees, all on the board, went to jail. Governance here means: who controls the company, and whose pockets does it serve?

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: Which executive does the handout send to prison in the Tyco row?

choices.text: Bernie Ebbers
Dennis Kozlowski
Barry Minkow
Albert Fall

questions.explanation:
Match the person to the company: Kozlowski–Tyco, Ebbers–WorldCom, Dunlap–Sunbeam, Minkow–ZZZZ Best, Fall–Teapot Dome.

Tyco’s flavor is conglomerate plus aggressive acquisition accounting, not WorldCom’s pure capitalization trick. Restatement, SEC, class actions, prison: the late-1990s/early-2000s enforcement package again.
questions.lesson: Tyco (2002) was a large conglomerate. It used aggressive merger accounting to increase earnings, plus other illicit practices. The company restated earnings and paid fines to settle SEC charges and class-action lawsuits. CEO Dennis Kozlowski and others went to prison. Merger accounting can become fraud when you twist purchase accounting, reserves, or “one-time” items to manufacture growth.

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: What new overseer did Sarbanes-Oxley create, and what else did the Act change according to the handout?

choices.text: The Federal Reserve; it set income-tax rates
The PCAOB; plus new rules on governance, internal control, and auditing
The RTC; plus junk-bond deregulation
Tammany Hall; plus CPA advertising rights

questions.explanation:
Before SOX, public-company auditors were largely self-regulated. After SOX, a public board inspects them.

Governance: boards and audit committees. Internal control: the FCPA idea, hardened. Auditing: standards and inspections. PCAOB: the institutional hammer.

Do not say SOX created FASB (1973) or the SEC (1934). SOX created the PCAOB in 2002.
questions.lesson: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX, 2002) is the statutory climax of the Enron/WorldCom era. After those scandals “and all the rest,” Congress passed financial reform: new rules on corporate governance, internal control, and auditing, and it created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB). The PCAOB is a nonprofit overseer, created by federal law, that sets and inspects public-company audit standards. It is not FASB.

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: Which pair of headline scandals does the handout name as the immediate backdrop for SOX?

choices.text: Ponzi and Teapot Dome
Enron and WorldCom
Ultramares and Salad Oil
Madoff and LTCM only

questions.explanation:
The handout’s own words: after Enron and WorldCom and all the rest, Congress passed reform.

“All the rest” is Adelphia, Tyco, and the 1997–1999 restatement wave. But if you must pick two names that sold SOX to the public, they are Enron and WorldCom.
questions.lesson: Name the 2001–2002 cascade in order: Regulation FD (2001) → Enron (2001) → WorldCom, Adelphia, Tyco (2002) → Sarbanes-Oxley and the PCAOB (2002).

questions.module: 2003–2006: The first scandals after SOX
questions.prompt: Why is HealthSouth specially labeled in this timeline?

choices.text: It was the first CPA licensing statute in New York
It is called the first post-Sarbanes-Oxley scandal; $2.5 billion restated for 2002 and bankruptcy in 2003
It successfully ended too-big-to-fail
It replaced the APB in 1973

questions.explanation:
If you thought SOX was a force field, HealthSouth is the counterexample, dated one year later.

The techniques mix Tyco-like merger accounting with a government-program twist: overbilling Medicare. $2.5 billion is larger than Waste Management’s or Sunbeam’s $1 billion-class restatements. Bankruptcy in 2003 closes the row.
questions.lesson: HealthSouth (2003) ran inpatient rehabilitation hospitals. The handout flags it as the first post-Sarbanes-Oxley scandal. Profits were kept up with aggressive merger accounting, overcharging Medicare, and other fraud. It restated $2.5 billion of 2002 earnings and declared bankruptcy in 2003. SOX did not make fraud impossible; it made the next fraud a test of the new law.

questions.module: 2003–2006: The first scandals after SOX
questions.prompt: What accounting hit did Fannie Mae take in 2004, and what happened to Fannie and Freddie in 2008?

choices.text: A $50 postal-coupon restatement; they were deported
Over $6 billion restated in 2004; both GSEs went into federal conservatorship in 2008
An $11 billion opex capitalization; both became PCAOB inspectors
A $1.6 billion SEC fine only, with no later takeover

questions.explanation:
Two dates, two problems.

2004: earnings were wrong, including derivatives. $6 billion is the restatement. 2008: they were undercapitalized on a mountain of mortgage risk, so the government seized them.

Conservatorship is not the RTC selling S&L branches, and not Lehman’s bankruptcy. It is “the feds run you now because your failure would wreck the mortgage market.”
questions.lesson: Fannie Mae and, to a lesser extent, Freddie Mac were government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) that bought and guaranteed mortgages. The handout calls them repeat violators of accounting rules, including ignoring derivative losses. In 2004 Fannie was forced to restate over $6 billion (the handout says “by the SC,” meaning the SEC). In 2008 both were placed into federal conservatorship: the government took them over to run them, without ordinary bankruptcy.

questions.module: 2003–2006: The first scandals after SOX
questions.prompt: What did the 2005 AIG chapter in the timeline include?

choices.text: A $180 billion TARP grant to homeowners
Internal-control weaknesses, a $1.6 billion fine, and criminal charges against several executives
The invention of junk bonds
Luca Pacioli’s publication in Venice

questions.explanation:
$1.6 billion (2005 fine) is not $180 billion (2008 equity bailout).

The 2005 story is books and controls. The 2008 story is that AIG had written enormous insurance-like protection on mortgage securities and could not pay. Students who blend the numbers fail the timeline.
questions.lesson: AIG (American International Group) was a giant insurer and a Dow Jones Industrial Average component. In 2005 it was cited for substantial internal-control weaknesses. An SEC fraud investigation produced a $1.6 billion fine and criminal charges against several executives. Remember this 2005 enforcement row separately from the 2008 $180 billion bailout. Same company, two chapters.

questions.module: 2003–2006: The first scandals after SOX
questions.prompt: What did the 2006 options scandal, at its core, involve?

choices.text: Confirming McKesson receivables
Backdating stock-option awards (and related tricks) to increase executive compensation
Filling tanks with water
Paying early Ponzi investors with new postal coupons

questions.explanation:
This is compensation fraud, not revenue fraud.

The accounting and disclosure issue is that the company understated pay. Spring-loading and speed vesting are cousins: still gaming the option’s value or timing. “Dozens of companies” means it was a practice, not one rogue firm.
questions.lesson: A stock option lets an executive buy shares at a set “strike” price. If you secretly pick a past date when the stock was cheap, you make the option more valuable: that is backdating. In 2006 the SEC found dozens of companies doing it to fatten pay. Other games followed: exercise backdating, spring-loading (timing grants before good news), and speed vesting (accelerating when options become exercisable). Several executives were prosecuted.

questions.module: 2003–2006: The first scandals after SOX
questions.prompt: What is the honest reading of 2003–2006 in this handout?

choices.text: SOX permanently ended corporate fraud, so the crisis of 2008 was unrelated
Fraud and control failures continued in hospitals, GSEs, a giant insurer, and executive pay, even after the PCAOB existed
The APB was restored to replace FASB
CPA exams were canceled

questions.explanation:
SOX is a response, not a cure-all.

The timeline refuses to stop at 2002. It marches through HealthSouth, Fannie, AIG, and options as a bridge into subprime. The profession’s new overseer is in place, and the scandals keep coming, now with more housing and more leverage mixed in.
questions.lesson: After SOX: HealthSouth (2003) proves scandals continue; Fannie’s 2004 restatement shows GSE accounting was rotten; AIG’s 2005 fine shows a Dow insurer’s controls failed; 2006 options backdating shows pay was being gamed. The next pages are housing.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: When does the handout say the subprime scandals started to unravel, and why?

choices.text: In 1896, because New York licensed CPAs
In 2007, as housing prices declined
In 1494, when Pacioli published
In 1934, when the SEC was created

questions.explanation:
Rising house prices hide bad loans: the borrower can refinance or sell. Falling prices reveal them.

Predatory lending is the origination sin. Structured finance is the laundering step (slice the pool, label the top slice “safe”). Speculation is the crowd that piled on. 2007 is the year the tide goes out.
questions.lesson: Subprime loans go to borrowers with weaker credit. The 2007–2008 scandal, in the handout, is a three-part manipulation: predatory lending (loans designed to fail or to strip equity), structured finance that made mortgage bundles look high quality, and widespread speculation. The structure started to unravel in 2007 as housing prices declined. When prices fall, the collateral is no longer there.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: How was Bear Stearns resolved in the timeline?

choices.text: It was allowed to fail, like Lehman later that year, with no help
J.P. Morgan acquired it after the feds agreed to cover up to $30 billion in toxic assets
It merged into Fannie Mae’s conservatorship
It became the PCAOB

questions.explanation:
Bear is “rescued by shotgun marriage.”

The buyer is J.P. Morgan. The public’s skin is up to $30 billion of the ugly assets. Contrast Lehman, a few months later: no buyer, no backstop, bankruptcy. The timeline wants you to feel that policy inconsistency, because markets felt it too.
questions.lesson: Bear Stearns was an investment bank that ran out of cash in March 2008: no liquidity to meet obligations. The Fed and Treasury engineered a rescue in which J.P. Morgan acquired Bear, and the government agreed to be responsible for up to $30 billion of toxic assets. Toxic assets here are mortgage-related positions nobody wanted to buy at yesterday’s prices.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: Why take Fannie and Freddie into conservatorship in 2008?

choices.text: They had just been created and needed a startup loan
They were failing GSEs with losses, negative equity, and trillions in mortgage securities and guarantees
They had only a Teapot Dome oil-lease problem
They refused to sit for CPA exams

questions.explanation:
Remember the 2004 restatement as a warning shot. 2008 is the solvency event.

Trillions of guarantees mean: if they fall over, mortgage finance in the United States seizes. Conservatorship is the tool chosen instead of Lehman-style bankruptcy.
questions.lesson: In summer 2008 the government put Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship. The handout says the GSEs had lost billions, had negative equity (liabilities bigger than assets), and sat on trillions of dollars of mortgage securities and guarantees. Negative equity plus a nationally important mortgage book is why they were taken over rather than left to ordinary failure.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: What does the handout say happened after Lehman was allowed to fail?

choices.text: Nothing; markets treated it as a small broker
Near-paralysis of global credit markets, Fed liquidity on a multi-trillion-dollar scale, and the creation of TARP
Immediate repeal of the Constitution
Pacioli republished Summa in Venice

questions.explanation:
Lehman is the timeline’s demonstration of “too big to fail” in the negative: they let it fail, and the credit system stopped.

That panic is why AIG is rescued days later, why TARP is jammed through Congress, and why Dodd-Frank in 2010 will claim it wants to end too-big-to-fail. Whether it did so is the last debate on the last page.
questions.lesson: After Bear was saved, Lehman Brothers was allowed to fail in 2008 (the handout says October; the bankruptcy filing was mid-September). It was the nation’s largest bankruptcy. The reaction was almost complete paralysis of global credit markets. That freeze required multi-trillion-dollar liquidity packages from the Federal Reserve and the creation of TARP.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: How large was the 2008 AIG bailout in the handout, and what was the purpose?

choices.text: $1.6 billion, same as the 2005 fine, to settle an advertising case
About $180 billion in equity, to avoid failure of the world’s largest insurer
$100 billion, the S&L taxpayer loss, paid to Minkow
$11 billion, WorldCom’s capitalized expenses, refunded to Ebbers

questions.explanation:
Keep AIG’s two numbers in separate pockets: $1.6 billion fine (2005) vs. $180 billion equity (2008).

Bear: $30 billion toxic-asset backstop for a buyer. AIG: $180 billion to own and stabilize the insurer. Lehman: $0, and a global seizure. Those three policy choices are the heart of the 2008 chapter.
questions.lesson: After Lehman, the government bailed out AIG with about $180 billion of equity so the world’s largest insurance company would not fail. AIG had sold protection on mortgage risks; when those risks went bad, AIG owed collateral it did not have. Equity from the government is ownership capital, not a small fine.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: What did TARP primarily do in practice, according to the handout?

choices.text: Funded the original New York CPA exam
Put capital into failing banks; help for mortgage holders was only limited
Created FASB to replace the APB
Deported Charles Ponzi

questions.explanation:
TARP is a bank-capital program that wore a homeowner label.

That gap matters for legitimacy: the public heard “save houses,” and much of the money recapitalized institutions. The Fed’s separate liquidity facilities (mentioned in the Lehman row) are not TARP. TARP is the congressional capital injection.
questions.lesson: TARP, the Troubled Asset Relief Program (2008), was sold after Treasury and Fed prodding. It provided billions of dollars of capital to failing banks. The bill was originally designed to bail out mortgage holders, which, the handout says, happened only to a limited extent. So the political story (help homeowners) and the operational story (recapitalize banks) diverged.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: How does Madoff’s scheme, in this timeline, differ from Ponzi’s 1920 operation?

choices.text: Madoff lasted 45 days and was deported to Italy
Madoff’s Ponzi ran for decades at multibillion scale and ended in 2008 with a 150-year sentence
Madoff only backdated stock options at HealthSouth
Madoff created the SEC in 1934

questions.explanation:
Same machine: pay old investors with new investors’ money until the inflow stops.

Different wrapper and duration. Ponzi’s wrapper was postal coupons and greed for a 50% sprint. Madoff’s wrapper was a famous market-maker’s reputation and a supposedly steady, impossible track record. The 2008 crash is what finally stopped the inflow. 150 years is the court’s way of saying the harm cannot be repaid in one lifetime.
questions.lesson: Bernard Madoff had been a NASDAQ innovator and trader. He also ran a multibillion-dollar Ponzi scheme for decades. When investor cash ran out in 2008, he confessed to fraud and theft and was sentenced to 150 years in jail. Compare Charles Ponzi (1920): months, millions, 50% in 45 days, deportation. Madoff: decades, billions, a respectable Wall Street face, 150 years.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: Which cluster of purposes does the handout quote for Dodd-Frank, and what is the handout’s closing note?

choices.text: To repeal CPA licensing; everyone agrees it worked perfectly
Stability, transparency, ending too-big-to-fail and bailouts, and consumer protection; effectiveness has been debated ever since
To create CAP and issue 51 ARBs
To lease Teapot Dome to oilmen

questions.explanation:
Dodd-Frank is a mission statement plus an argument.

The mission: no more Lehman-style chaos, no more AIG-style rescues, no more predatory lending without a cop. The argument: maybe those goals conflict, and maybe the statute did not deliver them.

The timeline ends on that unresolved note on purpose. History, in this course, does not close with a bow.
questions.lesson: Dodd-Frank (2010) is the crisis statute, as SOX was the Enron statute. The handout quotes its purposes: promote financial stability by improving accountability and transparency; end “too big to fail”; protect taxpayers by ending bailouts; protect consumers from abusive financial-services practices; and other purposes. Then the last line: the potential effectiveness has been debated ever since.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: Which 2008 sequence matches the handout?

choices.text: Dodd-Frank, then Pacioli, then Tammany Hall
Bear rescued, GSEs seized, Lehman failed, AIG bailed out, TARP passed
Ultramares, then McKesson, then CAP
HealthSouth, then ZZZZ Best, then Sherman

questions.explanation:
Order is the exam.

If you put Lehman before Bear, you miss why people thought Bear was the template. If you put TARP before Lehman, you miss why Congress finally voted the money. If you confuse AIG’s 2005 fine with the 2008 bailout, you miss the difference between an enforcement case and a systemic rescue.
questions.lesson: Put 2007–2010 in order: housing prices fall and subprime unravels (2007) → Bear is sold with a $30B backstop (March 2008) → Fannie/Freddie conservatorship (summer 2008) → Lehman fails and credit freezes → AIG gets ~$180B → TARP recapitalizes banks (homeowner relief limited) → Madoff’s cash runs out → Dodd-Frank (2010) tries to legislate an end to the era.

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: What pattern should you expect whenever the timeline shows a famous scandal?

choices.text: The profession abolishes double-entry bookkeeping
Public outrage and institutional failure are followed, sooner or later, by a new licensing rule, disclosure law, audit procedure, or overseer
The Constitution is rewritten from scratch each time
GAAP is replaced by junk bonds

questions.explanation:
You are not memorizing 46 trivia cards. You are learning a civic loop.

Abuse → discovery → outrage → institution. The institutions pile up (SEC, FASB, PCAOB) instead of replacing the need for judgment. Continental Vending and HealthSouth exist to remind you that a new rule does not end the loop.
questions.lesson: A repeating engine in this timeline is: a visible abuse, then a new law or standard. Political machines and Teapot Dome are public corruption. Ponzi and Madoff are fake returns. McKesson is fake assets. Enron/WorldCom are fake earnings. Subprime is fake loan quality. Each time, someone writes a rule: CPA licenses, Sherman, the Fed, the SEC, inventory observation, FASB, FCPA, SOX/PCAOB, Dodd-Frank.

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: Match the crisis statute to its core institutional move.

choices.text: 1933–34: PCAOB; 2002: RTC; 2010: Tammany Hall
1933–34: SEC and disclosure; 2002: PCAOB and audit/governance/control rules; 2010: stability, too-big-to-fail, consumer protection
1933–34: junk bonds; 2002: salad oil; 2010: reply coupons
All three created FASB in different years

questions.explanation:
If you can make this match, you can navigate the whole handout.

SEC = markets and disclosure. PCAOB = public-company auditors. Dodd-Frank = banks, bailouts, and consumers. FASB is not in this triplet; it is the 1973 GAAP successor to the APB.
questions.lesson: Three statutes are easy to confuse because they all follow crises. 1933–34 Securities Acts: create the SEC, force disclosure after 1920s/crash abuses. 2002 SOX: create the PCAOB, tighten governance, controls, and audits after Enron/WorldCom. 2010 Dodd-Frank: financial-stability and too-big-to-fail agenda after 2008. Different villains, different tools.

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: Which list correctly separates GAAP-setting from audit oversight?

choices.text: PCAOB wrote ARBs in 1938; CAP inspects audits today
CAP then APB then FASB write GAAP; 1939 procedures respond to McKesson; PCAOB oversees public-company audits after SOX
The Fed writes GAAP; Tammany Hall inspects audits
Ultramares created FASB; Salad Oil created the SEC

questions.explanation:
Job, not acronym soup.

Who says how to measure? CAP/APB/FASB. Who said “actually look at inventory”? The 1939 audit committee after McKesson. Who inspects public-company auditors now? PCAOB. Who polices markets and disclosure? SEC. Keep those four jobs in four boxes and the timeline stops being a blur.
questions.lesson: GAAP writers in this timeline: Committee on Accounting Procedures (1938, ARBs) → Accounting Principles Board (1959, same problems) → FASB (1973, better process and public involvement). Audit-procedure shock: McKesson 1937 → Committee on Audit Procedures 1939 (observe inventory, confirm receivables). Public-company audit overseer: PCAOB (2002).

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: Which statement about auditor consequences is true in this handout?

choices.text: Auditors have never been sued or prosecuted
Civil liability was limited in Ultramares, criminal guilt still attached in Continental Vending, liability was eased in 1995, then public oversight tightened in 2002
After Ultramares, auditors were automatically liable to every stock trader in the world
Continental Vending abolished GAAS

questions.explanation:
Liability is a pendulum.

Too little, and careless or captured audits proliferate (the handout’s reading of the late 1990s). Too much, and firms may refuse useful work. Ultramares, Continental Vending, the 1995 Act, and SOX are four waypoints on that pendulum, not four names for the same event.
questions.lesson: Auditor legal risk swings. Ultramares (1924): negligent but not fraudulent → not liable to the lender. Continental Vending (1969): GAAS compliance did not block a criminal-fraud conviction. PSLRA (1995): Congress cuts civil liability, and the handout thinks audits got more aggressive. SOX (2002): inspections and control attestations raise the cost of a sloppy public-company audit again.

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: Which event is specifically about ending selective, insider-first earnings news?

choices.text: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890
Regulation FD in 2001
The Garn-St. Germain Act of 1982
CPA licensing in 1896

questions.explanation:
Sherman is monopoly. Garn-St. Germain is S&L deregulation. CPA licensing is who may call themselves an auditor. Regulation FD is the microphone: if it is material, put it on the public webcast.

The SEC of 1934 invented the idea of adequate public disclosure. FD is that idea applied to the analyst phone call.
questions.lesson: Several rows are about who hears the truth, not only whether the truth is in the footnotes. Tammany and Teapot Dome hide public deals. Regulation FD (2001) forbids whispering earnings to favorite analysts. SOX tries to make controls and audits more public. Dodd-Frank talks about transparency in the financial system. Disclosure is a running theme from 1934 through 2010.

questions.module: 1787–1896: A federal government, markets, and the first CPAs
questions.prompt: Which breakups does the handout cite as government antitrust wins?

choices.text: Enron and WorldCom
Northern Pacific Railroad and Rockefeller’s Standard Oil
Deloitte and Ernst & Young
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in 1890

questions.explanation:
Enron and WorldCom collapsed from scandal in 2001–2002; they were not Sherman Act breakups in 1890.

Northern Pacific and Standard Oil are the 19th-century trophies. They tell you why a federal government that can “function adequately” matters: it can take on the largest private organizations of its day.
questions.lesson: The Interstate Commerce Commission (1887) targeted railroads. Sherman (1890) targeted trusts. The concrete “wins” named in the handout are the breakup of the Northern Pacific Railroad and of Rockefeller’s Standard Oil. Those are demonstrations that federal law could actually dismember a private empire, not just pass a statute and hope.

questions.module: 1913–1924: Progressive reform, Ponzi, Teapot Dome, and Ultramares
questions.prompt: The Clayton Act belongs in which bundle?

choices.text: The 2002 SOX bundle with the PCAOB
The 1913–1914 Progressive reform bundle after the Pujo hearings
The 1982 S&L deregulation bundle
The 1920 Ponzi deportation bundle

questions.explanation:
Clayton is easy to lose in the list because it is not a new agency. It is more antitrust law.

Pujo hearings → 16th Amendment, Federal Reserve, FTC, Clayton. If you put Clayton in 2002, you have mixed Progressive trust-busting with post-Enron audit reform.
questions.lesson: The Clayton Act (1914) is additional antitrust law in the Pujo-era package, alongside the Fed, the FTC, and the income tax. It is not the 1933 Securities Act and not SOX. When you see 1913–1914, think: tax + central bank + competition agencies + tighter antitrust.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: Who sued the auditor in Ultramares, and in what role?

choices.text: The PCAOB, as inspector
Ultramares, as a lender that had relied on the audited statements
Charles Ponzi, as a competing accountant
The RTC, as conservator of an S&L

questions.explanation:
Name the plaintiff: Ultramares. Role: lender. Defendant auditor: Touche Niven. Defect: clean opinion, substantial fraud. Holding: negligence, not fraud, so no liability in that case.

If you remember only “some old lawsuit,” you will mix it with Continental Vending’s criminal case.
questions.lesson: An unqualified opinion is a clean opinion. In Ultramares it was issued despite fraud. The plaintiff was not a shareholder class in the modern sense; it was Ultramares the lender. Lenders care about solvency and collateral. That is why a clean opinion on cooked books is such a dangerous piece of paper: it is used to extend credit.

questions.module: 1963–1979: Salad oil, Continental Vending, FASB, FCPA, and lowballing
questions.prompt: Where do public-company internal-control requirements first show up as a statute in this timeline?

choices.text: In the Articles of Confederation
In the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977, alongside the anti-bribery rules
In Ponzi’s 1920 indictment
In the 1890 Sherman Act’s railroad appendix

questions.explanation:
