People think internal control begins in 2002 because that is when they memorized “Section 404.” This handout is older than that memory.

1977: Congress says public firms must have controls (and must not bribe foreign officials). 2002: Congress says prove it, and lets the PCAOB inspect the auditors who attest.
questions.lesson: Internal control is the company’s own machinery: approvals, recordkeeping, segregation of duties, safeguarding of assets. The FCPA (1977) put a federal internal-control mandate on public firms at the same moment it banned foreign bribery. SOX later makes managers and auditors report on those controls. FCPA is the ancestor; SOX is the reinforcement.

questions.module: 1982–1995: Deregulation, junk bonds, ZZZZ Best, and the S&L bailout
questions.prompt: Which pair does the handout present as professional-environment changes that may have weakened audits before the late-1990s scandals?

choices.text: McKesson inventory observation and receivable confirmation
The 1979 advertising-ban lift (lowballing / commodity pricing) and the 1995 reduction in auditor legal liability
The 1787 Constitution and the 16th Amendment
TARP and conservatorship

questions.explanation:
Fieldwork standards (observe, confirm) were supposed to make audits more substantive after 1939. Decades later, the business and legal environment may have pushed the other way: price the job like a commodity, and face less lawsuit risk if you miss a fraud.

That is the handout’s bridge from 1979/1995 into Waste Management, Sunbeam, Enron, and WorldCom.
questions.lesson: Lowballing (after 1979) is about winning the audit with a cheap bid. The 1995 litigation reform is about shrinking the chance that a cheap or aggressive audit ends in a ruinous lawsuit. The handout treats both as pressures that can reduce audit quality going into the late 1990s.

questions.module: 1997–2001: Late-1990s accounting failures and Regulation FD
questions.prompt: Which matching of 1997–1998 fraud style is correct?

choices.text: Waste Management: postal coupons; Sunbeam: Teapot Dome leases; Cendant: Sherman breakups
Waste Management: PPE/earnings; Sunbeam: revenue recognition under Dunlap; Cendant: inherited CUC fraud after an acquisition
All three were S&L conservatorships
All three were caused by Regulation FD

questions.explanation:
Sorting by mechanism is how you stop mixing the names.

PPE assumptions vs. revenue tricks vs. buying a dirty target. Regulation FD is 2001 and is about fair disclosure, not about these restatements.
questions.lesson: Waste Management = PPE and mixed earnings inflation, then failure after $1B+ restatements. Sunbeam = Dunlap, fake revenue, $1B write-off, bankruptcy. Cendant = bought CUC’s pre-existing fraud. Three styles of late-1990s corporate accounting failure, all before Enron’s SPE cathedral.

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: A company records ordinary operating costs as long-lived assets to hide a profit collapse of about $11 billion. Which timeline scandal is that?

choices.text: Enron 2001
WorldCom 2002
Teapot Dome 1920s
ZZZZ Best 1986

questions.explanation:
WorldCom’s simplicity is the point. You do not need a derivative model. You need a journal entry that turns a cost into an asset.

Enron needed a web of entities. Adelphia needed a family. Tyco needed merger accounting. Match the method, then the name, then the year, then SOX.
questions.lesson: Special purpose entities, derivatives, and trading-profit games (Enron) are not the same as capitalizing line costs (WorldCom). If an exam stem says “simple fraud” and “operating expenses as capital assets,” it is WorldCom. If it says “pipeline company turned high-tech trader” and “SPEs,” it is Enron.

questions.module: 2001–2002: Enron, WorldCom, and Sarbanes-Oxley
questions.prompt: After Enron and WorldCom, who was created to oversee public-company auditors?

choices.text: The Committee on Accounting Procedures
The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board
Tammany Hall
The Interstate Commerce Commission

questions.explanation:
CAP is 1938 GAAP. Tammany is 19th-century machine politics. The ICC is 1887 railroads. PCAOB is 2002 audit oversight.

Say it as a sentence: Congress did not trust the profession to inspect itself on public companies anymore.
questions.lesson: SOX’s PCAOB is to auditors what the SEC is to markets: a public overseer created after a scandal cluster. The SEC is 1934. The PCAOB is 2002. FASB remains the GAAP writer. Mixing those three is the most common timeline error in the course.

questions.module: 2003–2006: The first scandals after SOX
questions.prompt: Which pairing of “early warning” and “crisis ending” is accurate?

choices.text: HealthSouth 2003 restatement, then HealthSouth becomes the Fed in 2008
Fannie’s 2004 restatement then 2008 conservatorship; AIG’s 2005 fine then 2008 equity bailout
Ultramares 1924, then Ultramares buys Lehman
Ponzi 1920, then Ponzi writes Dodd-Frank

questions.explanation:
The handout is teaching you to read early enforcement as a credit event that has not happened yet.

If the accounting already cannot be trusted (Fannie) or the controls already failed (AIG), a housing collapse will not be a mild earnings miss. It will be a public rescue.
questions.lesson: Fannie (2004 restatement over $6B; 2008 conservatorship) and AIG (2005 $1.6B fine; 2008 $180B bailout) are two-step tragedies. First the books and controls are shown to be weak. Later the mortgage crash turns those firms into wards of the state. HealthSouth (2003) does not get a 2008 sequel in this handout; it is the immediate post-SOX corporate scandal.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: Which firm was allowed to fail in 2008, producing the nation’s largest bankruptcy in this timeline?

choices.text: Bear Stearns
Lehman Brothers
AIG
J.P. Morgan

questions.explanation:
Bear lived inside J.P. Morgan. AIG lived on Treasury/Fed equity. Fannie and Freddie lived in conservatorship. Lehman died.

The death is what froze credit. That freeze is why “too big to fail” becomes the political slogan Dodd-Frank tries to retire.
questions.lesson: Three 2008 official endings: Bear is bought (with a public backstop). Fannie and Freddie are conserved. Lehman is bankrupt. AIG is nationalized in all but name via $180B of equity. TARP then recapitalizes banks. That is not one policy. It is five, in a panic.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: How should you answer a question about TARP’s original design versus what it mainly delivered?

choices.text: Original design: PCAOB inspections; delivered: CPA licenses
Original design: bail out mortgage holders; delivered: billions of capital to failing banks, with only limited homeowner help
Original design: salad-oil inspections; delivered: ARBs
Original design: junk bonds; delivered: Teapot Dome leases

questions.explanation:
Read the stem. “Originally designed” points to homeowners. “Provided billions of dollars of capital” points to banks.

The handout is almost sarcastic: the political wrapping and the wiring diagram were not the same. That is part of why crisis policy stayed controversial into Dodd-Frank.
questions.lesson: TARP’s original public design, in the handout, was help for mortgage holders. In operation it was capital for failing banks, with only limited homeowner relief. If a question asks what TARP “was originally designed” to do, the answer is mortgage holders. If it asks what TARP “provided,” the answer is bank capital.

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: Why is Madoff placed in 2008 next to Lehman, AIG, and TARP rather than next to the 1920 Ponzi row only?

choices.text: Because Madoff invented the Federal Reserve that year
Because the 2008 cash-flow freeze is when his decades-long Ponzi ran out of new money and collapsed into view
Because he was Interior Secretary Albert Fall
Because he wrote the 51 ARBs

questions.explanation:
A Ponzi needs new cash. 2008 is when investors needed their cash back and stopped supplying more.

The handout could have listed Madoff only as a cousin of Ponzi. By dating him 2008, it ties a classic confidence game to a modern liquidity crisis. Both are “the money was never really there.”
questions.lesson: Ponzi 1920 and Madoff 2008 bookend the timeline’s pure investment frauds. In between, most scandals are about companies’ own financial statements (McKesson, Waste Management, Enron, WorldCom) or about public officials (Tammany, Teapot Dome) or about financial-system leverage (LTCM, S&Ls, subprime). Madoff arriving in the same year as Lehman and TARP shows that a crash reveals more than one kind of rot.

questions.module: The big picture: how the timeline fits together
questions.prompt: Which is the best one-sentence summary of Handout #2’s U.S. timeline?

choices.text: Accounting history is only the biography of Luca Pacioli
U.S. accounting, auditing, and disclosure rules are built, scandal by scandal, on top of federal power, licensed professionals, and periodic public backlashes
Nothing important happens after 1896
The PCAOB existed before the Constitution

questions.explanation:
You now have a story, not a heap of dates.

Federal power makes rules possible. Scandals make new rules necessary. CPAs, GAAP boards, the SEC, and the PCAOB are the institutional sediment of those scandals. Dodd-Frank’s last line is the course’s attitude: we keep arguing whether the latest sediment is enough.
questions.lesson: If you are cold-starting this course, here is the spine of Handout #2’s U.S. timeline: build a federal government (1787); fight corruption and monopoly (Tammany, Sherman); license CPAs (1896); tax income and create the Fed (1913–14); invent the SEC after the crash (1933–34); force auditors to look (McKesson/1939); professionalize GAAP (CAP/APB/FASB); criminalize bribery and require controls (FCPA); watch audit pricing and liability shift (1979, 1995); endure a scandal wave (1997–2002); create the PCAOB (SOX); then watch housing leverage take down banks, insurers, and GSEs (2007–10) until Dodd-Frank.

questions.module: 1933–1959: New Deal, the SEC, and the first GAAP and audit rules
questions.prompt: What does the handout claim about CAP’s 51 ARBs?

choices.text: They were all repealed the day the SEC opened
They represented many fundamental accounting standards still in use, though particulars changed over time
They were criminal indictments of Price Waterhouse
They created TARP

questions.explanation:
Old does not mean irrelevant.

The point of putting 1938–59 in a professionalism course is that today’s accountant still lives inside decisions made when GAAP was first being written down. FASB changed the government of the rules. It did not vaporize the idea of the rules.
questions.lesson: Fifty-one Accounting Research Bulletins in twenty years (1938–1959) means CAP was busy. The handout says those ARBs became many of the fundamental standards still in use, even though particulars changed. When FASB later codified GAAP, a lot of that DNA was still CAP-era thinking about assets, liabilities, and matching.

questions.module: 2007–2010: Housing, bailouts, Madoff, and Dodd-Frank
questions.prompt: How does the handout want you to treat claims that Dodd-Frank “solved” 2008?

choices.text: As settled fact, because the timeline ends with a trophy
Cautiously: the statute announced those goals, and “the potential effectiveness has been debated ever since”
As irrelevant, because accounting history ended in 1896
As proof that the Articles of Confederation were restored

questions.explanation:
The last human sentence of the handout is a shrug, not a celebration.

Learn the quoted purposes so you can recognize them on an exam. Then remember that this course treats financial reform as unfinished. That attitude is part of the content.
questions.lesson: Dodd-Frank’s quoted purposes include ending bailouts and ending too-big-to-fail. The 2008 rows you just studied are those problems in the flesh: Bear backed, Lehman dropped, AIG owned, TARP filled, GSEs conserved. The Act is a promise about the next crisis. The handout refuses to say the promise has been kept.
